before.text: When you scrape your knee, skin cells around the wound divide to replace the ones you lost.
Each new cell carries the same 46 chromosomes as the cell it came from.
So how does one cell become two identical cells?
Think of a library opening a second branch.
It photocopies every book, clips each copy to its original, then sends one of each pair to each branch.
In a cell, the books are chromosomes, and each clipped pair is two sister chromatids.
The two branches are the daughter cells, and each gets the full collection.
Here is the whole process, left to right.
It starts before mitosis, in interphase, when the cell copies all its DNA.
A common mistake is to think DNA is copied during mitosis itself.
But the copying is done in interphase, and mitosis only separates the copies.
Next comes prophase, when the chromosomes coil up and the nuclear envelope breaks down.
Then spindle fibers grow out from the two poles of the cell.
Up close, each copied chromosome is two sister chromatids, joined at the centromere.
That's a book clipped to its copy.
Spindle fibers from opposite poles attach there, one to each sister chromatid.
So each sister is tied to a different pole.
Back in the row, metaphase comes next.
The chromosomes line up single file across the middle of the cell.
With fibers from both poles pulling on every chromosome, what happens when the sisters let go?
They split apart, and each one is pulled to the opposite pole.
That's anaphase, as the spindle fibers shorten and drag the chromatids along.
So each pole ends up with one copy of every chromosome, like each branch getting one book from every pair.
Back in the row, telophase follows, and a new nucleus forms around each set.
Then cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm, as a cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two.
That leaves two daughter cells, each with the same chromosomes as the parent.
Now, what happens if one pair of sister chromatids fails to separate in anaphase?
Both chromatids get pulled to the same pole.
So one daughter cell gets an extra chromosome, and the other is missing one.
The two cells are no longer identical.
So the cell copies every chromosome, then pulls the copies apart so each new cell gets a full set.
That's how one skin cell at your knee becomes two identical cells, each with the same 46 chromosomes.
